title: Comparative Forms: -er, More and Irregular Changes
summary: Build natural comparative forms to describe differences in size, cost, quality and manner. Use -er with short words, -ier with many two-syllable -y words, more with long adjectives and -ly adverbs, and irregular forms such as better and worse.
learningObjectives: Form comparatives with -er and apply common final-e, consonant-doubling and -y-to-ier spelling changes.
Use more before longer adjectives and adverbs ending in -ly, avoiding double comparative marking.
Recognise two-syllable adjectives that permit either -er or more.
Use better, worse, farther and further accurately, including further for additional information.

explanation.heading: Why we use comparative forms
explanation.body: A comparative describes a quality or manner relative to another person, thing or time. The second point of comparison may appear after than or be clear from context. For many short adjectives, add -er to the base form. The form identifies a difference, but does not by itself say how large the difference is.
explanation.example: Our replacement router is faster than the previous model.

explanation.heading: Short adjectives and spelling patterns
explanation.body: Add -er to most one-syllable adjectives: light → lighter and tall → taller. If the word ends in silent -e, add only -r: safe → safer. A short stressed vowel before one final consonant may require doubling the consonant: big → bigger. Two-syllable words ending in consonant + y usually change -y to -ier: busy → busier and easy → easier.
explanation.example: The new storage box is bigger but easier to carry.

explanation.heading: Use more with long adjectives and -ly adverbs
explanation.body: Most adjectives with two or more syllables take more rather than -er, especially longer ones such as efficient, reliable and expensive. Adverbs ending in -ly also generally take more: more carefully, more clearly, more slowly. Do not combine more with an -er ending on the same word. Short adverbs such as fast often use -er.
explanation.example: The revised instructions explain the procedure more clearly.

explanation.heading: Flexible two-syllable adjectives
explanation.body: Some two-syllable adjectives allow both an -er comparative and a more comparative. Common examples include clever, narrow, quiet, shallow and simple. One form may sound more natural in a particular sentence, but both can be grammatically acceptable. By contrast, standard usage normally prefers more with adjectives such as reliable or complicated.
explanation.example: The side entrance is quieter than the main doorway.

explanation.heading: Irregular forms and the special meaning of further
explanation.body: Good and the adverb well change to better; bad and badly change to worse. Far has two comparative forms, farther and further, for greater physical distance. Further also means additional, for example further details or further discussion; farther does not normally have that meaning. These irregular forms cannot be produced by simply adding more or -er.
explanation.example: We need further information before deciding which option is better.

left.label: -er / -ier
left.example: This hallway is narrower than the other one.
left.note: Narrow is one of the two-syllable adjectives that accepts narrower.

right.label: More + adjective
right.example: This entrance is more accessible than the other one.
right.note: The longer adjective accessible takes more, not an -er ending.

left.label: Farther / further for distance
left.example: The pharmacy is farther along the road.
left.note: Both farther and further can describe physical distance.

right.label: Further = additional
right.example: Please send further details by Friday.
right.note: Only further normally means additional in this usage.

examples.sentence: The second draft is clearer than the first.
examples.note: Clear is a short adjective and commonly uses the -er comparative.

examples.sentence: The corridor became busier after the doors opened.
examples.note: Busy changes its final y to i before -er.

examples.sentence: Could you explain that rule more slowly?
examples.note: An -ly adverb generally forms its comparative with more.

examples.sentence: This replacement part is more durable than the old one.
examples.note: The multisyllabic adjective durable takes more.

examples.sentence: Her second attempt went better than her first.
examples.note: Better is the irregular comparative of well when describing how an action goes.

commonMistakes.incorrect: This ticket is more cheap than the other one.
commonMistakes.correct: This ticket is cheaper than the other one.
commonMistakes.why: The short adjective cheap normally takes -er rather than more.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The meeting started earlyer than expected.
commonMistakes.correct: The meeting started earlier than expected.
commonMistakes.why: Change the final -y in early to -i before adding -er.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The backup process is reliabler now.
commonMistakes.correct: The backup process is more reliable now.
commonMistakes.why: Reliable uses more in the usual comparative pattern.
Good has the irregular comparative better, not gooder.

studyTips: Sort ten adjectives into short -er forms, -y-to-ier forms and more + adjective forms; read the pairs aloud.
When you write a comparison, check that you have not used both more and an -er ending on the same adjective.
Make a short irregular-form reference card for good/well → better, bad/badly → worse and far → farther/further.

exercises.prompt: The second package weighs less. It is ___ than the first package.
exercises.feedback: Light is a short adjective, so the comparative is lighter.

exercises.prompt: Our new booking system is ___ than the old one.
exercises.feedback: Efficient is a longer adjective and forms its comparative with more.

exercises.prompt: The morning class starts at eight, but the afternoon class begins at ten. The morning class starts ___.
exercises.feedback: Early becomes earlier; the -y changes to -i before -er.

exercises.prompt: After the repair, the signal is ___ than before.
exercises.feedback: Good has the irregular comparative better.

exercises.prompt: This path is ___ than the main road. (short; write one comparative adjective)
exercises.feedback: Use -er to form shorter from the one-syllable adjective short.

exercises.prompt: Please speak ___ so the visitors can follow your explanation. (slowly; comparative form)
exercises.feedback: Most -ly adverbs, including slowly, use more to form the comparative.

exercises.prompt: The office has become ___ since the additional staff arrived. (busy; comparative form)
exercises.feedback: Busy ends in consonant + y, so replace y with i and add -er.

exercises.prompt: The report is incomplete. We need ___ details before making a decision. (additional; use the comparative of far)
exercises.feedback: Further can mean additional; farther is generally used for physical distance.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: This coat is more warm than my old one.
acceptedAnswers: This coat is warmer than my old one.
exercises.feedback: Warm is a one-syllable adjective and normally takes the -er comparative warmer.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The performance began earlyer than we expected.
acceptedAnswers: The performance began earlier than we expected.
exercises.feedback: Early changes to earlier, not earlyer.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The weather was badder on Sunday than on Saturday.
acceptedAnswers: The weather was worse on Sunday than on Saturday.
exercises.feedback: Bad has the irregular comparative worse.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The presenter explained the process more carefullyer this time.
acceptedAnswers: The presenter explained the process more carefully this time.
exercises.feedback: Use more with the adverb carefully; do not add -er to an -ly adverb.

speakingExercises.prompt: Compare these two items in one sentence. Facts: the blue suitcase; light; the red suitcase. Start with “The blue suitcase” and use lighter than.
acceptedAnswers: The blue suitcase is lighter than the red suitcase.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use one sentence to compare the two options. Facts: the new route; more direct; the old route. Begin with “The new route”.
acceptedAnswers: The new route is more direct than the old route.
speakingExercises.feedback: Direct is naturally compared using more direct.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask one complete yes/no question comparing train and bus speed. Begin with “Is the train” and end with “the bus”. Use faster than.
acceptedAnswers: Is the train faster than the bus?
speakingExercises.feedback: Fast forms faster, and than introduces the comparison.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct this sentence aloud, keeping the same meaning: “This watch is expensiver than mine.”
acceptedAnswers: This watch is more expensive than mine.
speakingExercises.feedback: Expensive is a long adjective and takes more instead of -er.

speakingExercises.prompt: Last month the service was bad; this month it is even worse. Say one sentence beginning “The service” and using worse than last month.
acceptedAnswers: The service is worse than last month.
speakingExercises.feedback: The comparative of bad is worse, not badder.

speakingExercises.prompt: You need additional details to choose a supplier. Make one sentence starting with “I need” and containing “further details before I decide”.
acceptedAnswers: I need further details before I decide.
speakingExercises.feedback: Further means additional when it modifies information or details.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences from these facts. First: this chair; lighter; that chair. Second: this chair; more comfortable; that chair. Begin both sentences with “This chair”.
acceptedAnswers: This chair is lighter than that chair. This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
speakingExercises.feedback: Lighter uses -er, whereas comfortable takes more.

speakingExercises.prompt: A speaker is talking too quickly for you. Make a polite request using exactly the words “Could you speak more slowly, please?”
acceptedAnswers: Could you speak more slowly, please?
speakingExercises.feedback: The adverb slowly forms its comparative with more.

listeningExercises.audioText: The tram takes twenty minutes, while the bus takes thirty-five. I will take the faster option.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which form of transport gets the speaker there sooner?
listeningExercises.feedback: The tram takes twenty minutes, compared with thirty-five minutes for the bus.

listeningExercises.audioText: The silver laptop is cheaper, but it is also heavier than the black one.
listeningExercises.prompt: What disadvantage does the cheaper laptop have?
choices: It is less expensive to repair.
listeningExercises.feedback: Although the cheaper laptop costs less, the speaker says it is heavier.

listeningExercises.audioText: The new printer works more reliably when connected by cable.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word comparative phrase heard immediately after “works”.
listeningExercises.feedback: The -ly adverb reliably takes more in the comparative.

listeningExercises.audioText: I thought the climb would be difficult, but it was worse than I expected.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the actual climb compare with the speaker’s expectation?
listeningExercises.feedback: Worse than I expected describes a more difficult experience.

listeningExercises.audioText: The station hotel charges one hundred and twenty pounds, but the one outside the centre costs eighty.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which hotel costs less per night?
listeningExercises.feedback: The hotel outside the centre costs eighty pounds; the other costs one hundred and twenty.

listeningExercises.audioText: I used to cycle slowly on this road, but I ride faster now.
listeningExercises.prompt: What has changed about the speaker’s cycling?
choices: They cycle at a higher speed now.
listeningExercises.feedback: The contrast between slowly before and faster now indicates increased speed.

listeningExercises.audioText: The course begins earlier on Fridays than on Tuesdays.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single comparative word heard immediately after “begins”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Earlier is the comparative of early and signals an earlier starting time.

listeningExercises.audioText: My shoulder feels better since I changed my desk setup.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the one-word comparative adjective heard immediately after “feels”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Better is the irregular comparative of good in the expression feels better.
